author: Feven Merid
title: Where the mouse eats the cat
content:
“Welcome to the Central Prison of Douala,” La PJ, an inmate and a star of the documentary 

Jail Time Records

, says in an opening scene of the film. “The place where the mouse eats the cat.” Dione Roach, one of the film’s directors, offered me an interpretation: “The world is upside down in prison; the mouse can be more shrewd,” she said. The intimate glimpse into the Central Prison of Douala, also known as New Bell Prison, does indeed reveal an upside-down world. Like many prisons, its inmates recreate the contours of outside life on the inside, but in New Bell it’s taken to another level. There are actual neighborhoods like the Latin Quarter, home to the Emperor and his gang known as the Latinos, and the Base, where the prisoners who make up the quasi police squad reside. There’s a marketplace for people to sell fried foods and taxis, except these taxis are inmates who swiftly run through the congested prison to hand-deliver messages. They even have a “homeless” population, those who must sleep outside in the courtyard because there aren’t enough beds. Their neighborhood is dubbed House of the Penguins.

This all comes into focus when you learn New Bell is notoriously overcrowded — it was built for 800 people but currently holds almost 6,000. Thus, the prison has been transformed into a mini city, colloquially referred to by inmates as the 11th province of Cameroon (there a

author: Husam Mahjoub
title: The war Abu Dhabi didn’t need to fight
content:
Several outside actors have stoked the flames of war in Sudan, but none has had as great an impact as the United Arab Emirates. The evidence of its destructive role is overwhelming, but the Gulf kingdom’s Western allies have turned a blind eye to it.

At one time or another, Sudanese governments have hosted, armed, or tolerated rebels and opposition groups from all of the country’s neighbors, from Egypt and Libya to Uganda and Ethiopia. Sudan’s neighbors have repaid the favor, and a range of outside actors are now involved in the Sudanese civil war.

Key supporters of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) include Chad, Ethiopia, Uganda, Kenya, and South Sudan. Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Eritrea support the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the de facto government. Among all the external actors, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) is the most consequential, even though it has the least reason to be involved.

Every other external actor has a stake in Sudan that derives from geography, security exposure, or the influx of Sudanese refugees. Even Saudi Arabia, while not a land neighbor, shares the Red Sea coastline with Sudan and has a direct interest in stabilizing its western maritime frontier.

The UAE has no security interest, no shared border or river, and no reason to be concerned about refugees reaching Emirati territory. We can only understand its role in Sudan as part of a broader subimpe

author: Yatta Zoker
title: We are oil to you
content:
I’m exhausted. As are many of my peers.

When I was in my 20s and more spiritually adventurous, I would obsess over the 27 club.

During this time, I was opening for Sun Ra Arkestra and floating in the tradition of Black spiritual music. Mostly by accident.

I had a theory at the time that the story of Robert Johnson meeting a man at the crossroads and receiving the knowledge of how to play the guitar was actually about Elegba.

And that at 27, musicians had to decide whether to be in collaboration with the devil or choose another way.

A crossroads. A coming of age. A portal.

No wonder we are exhausted.

As musicians, we are in the business of energy.

Performances can be athletic, like a windmill. Poems, singing, and playing an instrument can generate energy as we receive inspiration like solar panels hearing instructions from the sun.

On the other side of things, there is the audience.

Depending on the context, the relationship between performer and audience can be life-giving or extractive. I’ve played festivals in Europe that have made me feel like my soul material is being mined.

I think of singers who have sedated themselves to stay alive but end up dead.

*

As artists who are children of immigrants, some of us have chosen a path different from our parents.

author: Michal Petros
title: Who gets to speak for Eritrea?
content:
Eritrea made its Miss World debut earlier this month, becoming one of the newest countries to join the competition since its founding in 1951. Miss Eritrea Snit Tewoldemedhin not only represented the country on this global platform for the first time — she won the 

People’s Choice Award

. This achievement is a remarkable demonstration of Eritrean diaspora mobilization, but it’s not what stuck with me following the competition. In reality, the last beauty pageant I watched was probably 

Miss Congeniality

, but as an Eritrean, it was impossible not to notice the paradox of Eritreans voting for the first time from a scattered diaspora, while those inside the country remain largely shut out of participation due to severe restrictions on internet access. It was equally impossible to overlook the irony of Miss Eritrea wearing a newspaper gown while representing a country with no freedom of the press.

Following 30 years of struggle, Africa’s longest war for independence, Eritrea officially gained sovereignty from neighboring Ethiopia in 1993. Since then, the country has remained a one-party state with no formal elections since independence and no free press since 2001. While the world’s attention was on the September 11 attacks in the US, Eritrea 

shut down

author: Garhe Osiebe
title: The political economy of romance
content:
If there was any doubt that “billing” has become central to Nigerian conversations about dating, money, and gender, eLDee the Don’s return to music has supplied a new soundtrack.

On July 25, 2026, Olanrewaju Dabiri, better known as eLDee the Don, returned from a lengthy recording hiatus with 

“I Wish You Well.” 

The rapper, singer, producer, and record executive has long used popular music to comment on Nigerian social life. This time, his subject is not electoral politics or poor governance, but the expectation that a man who expresses romantic interest should also finance a woman’s needs, wants, and lifestyle.

eLDee occupies an important place in the history of Nigerian popular music. Through the Trybesmen and the broader Da Trybe movement, he helped shape Nigerian hip-hop in the late 1990s and 2000s. Songs including “Plenty Nonsense,” “I Go Yarn,” “Bosi Gbangba,” “Big Boy,” and “One Day” combined entertainment with sharp observations about social aspiration, politics, and everyday life.

“I Wish You Well” continues that tradition with humor. Assisted by comedian Lasisi Elenu, eLDee narrates an encounter with a woman he has barely met. She first asks for a loan, claiming that her car has been towed and that rent is due. The requests soon expand to travel, designer goods, and other markers of luxury consumption.

author: Aidan Huang
title: People have to be treated as people
content:
From the airplane window, the land appeared almost uniformly yellow, stretched flat and uninterrupted beneath the wing. It was not the yellow of sunlight, but of dust and sand pressed into a vast plain, where roads were barely distinguishable from the earth around them. As the plane descended, the color did not change — it only grew closer. When the cabin door finally opened, heat rushed in immediately, dense and unapologetic, wrapping itself around the body before there was time to adjust. Outside, people moved through the glare wearing long sleeves, as if skin here had learned its own rules. Motorcycles dominated the roads, fast and loosely choreographed, riders weaving through traffic without helmets, without hesitation. Cars sped past on sand-colored streets, engines loud, windows open. I was driven through the city in a modest vehicle by a local professor — someone widely respected, I was later told — yet the ride itself felt precarious, carried forward by momentum more than by control. Only later did I begin to name the place where all of this was unfolding: N’Djamena, Chad.

Approaching N’Djamena from the air.

author: Ayoola Babalola
title: Too big to regulate
content:
In September 2024, Nigeria achieved something it had been promised for decades: the Dangote Petroleum Refinery began producing petrol on Nigerian soil. At 650,000 barrels per day, 

the largest single-train refinery on earth

, it was a genuine industrial landmark.

Yet, by early 2026, Nigerian consumers were paying petrol prices roughly 12 percent above what competitive imports would have cost, according to a shelved 

World Bank report

.

It is well argued by 

scholars

 that Nigerian merchant capital did not emerge organically from agricultural surpluses or small manufacturing. It was shaped, from the colonial era onward, by three distinctive features: import-substitution policies that protected specific domestic interests; an oil economy that concentrated state revenues in few hands; and a “political settlement,” in the words of economist and professor Mushtaq Khan, that tied business access to political proximity rather than competitive performance.

The 

Dantata

 family were among the trading families of northern Nigeria, enriched under colonial commodity boards that set paltry prices paid to farmers for export crops, with the boards accumulating surpluses that sometimes exceeded 100 percent of expected earnings. author: Richard Seymour
title: The extinction pitch
content:
It seems a strange publicity gambit for an industry to assert that its own product could wipe out humanity. In the lingo of our evolving tech empire, though, this is exactly what is meant by “criti-hype.” The term was coined by Lee Vinsel at Virginia Tech, who defined it as “criticism that both feeds and feeds on hype.”

When Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic recently, he claimed that there is a high chance that AI could develop into a superintelligence that escapes human control, triggering a sequence that causes human extinction. Evan Hubinger, who remains with the company, backed him up, saying that Anthropic is trying to prevent this but hasn’t dealt with the problem yet. Hubinger put the likelihood of AI-driven human extinction at greater than 10 percent in the next decade.

Why would a senior employee at a tech giant make an officially sanctioned, even approved, statement like this? I’ll come back to that. First, let’s unpack the theory of how AI could kill all humans.

The basic idea, from philosopher Nick Bostrom onward, is that the machine can acquire capabilities independently of whether it acquires ethical goals, or whether those goals are properly aligned with those of its designers. author: Ngozi Nwosu-Juba
title: Who profits from ‘saving’ women?
content:
During a recent dialogue convened by Liberation Alliance Africa’s 

Building Knowledge Bridges Community of Practice on Recentering African Feminist Epistemologies to Prevent and Respond to Sexual Violence

, bringing together activists, writers, and independent researchers from across the continent, an important and thought-provoking conversation emerged. While participants acknowledged the significant contributions of civil society organizations, development agencies, and other actors in advancing efforts to end violence against women and girls, there was also a collective reflection on the ways in which this support is framed and delivered.

I was struck by how this discussion raised critical questions about funding priorities, whose interests are ultimately served, who benefits most from existing interventions, and whether the structures and language designed to address violence may, in some instances, inadvertently reproduce inequalities or overlook the needs and voices of those most affected. The conversation challenged me to think beyond the availability of resources and examine the political, economic, and institutional dynamics that shape responses to violence against women and girls across the continent.

In my early days in feminist activism, I often highlighted to funders how our interventions had shifted away from speaking on behalf of women to “giving them voice.”

author: Sushovan Dhar
title: Roaches in revolt
content:
In May, hearing a routine case, the Chief Justice of India remarked from the bench that the country had “youngsters like cockroaches”: young people who, finding no work, become media people and activists and attack everybody. He called them parasites of society.

Within a day, a 30-year-old graduate had founded the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a straight parody of the BJP’s name. 

Membership criteria

: unemployed, lazy, permanently online, and able to complain professionally. 

Slogan

: Voice of the Lazy and Unemployed. Within three days, the account gained 3 million followers; within five days, it surpassed the governing party in followers; and by July, the total reached 22 million.

On 25 July, India’s Education Minister resigned; the first time in 12 years of Narendra Modi’s government that a street movement had removed a member of the cabinet. The organization that removed him was eight weeks old; it had no members, no funds, no offices, no registration as a political party and no program beyond satire.

That is what needs explaining: not the resignation, which was a tactical retreat, but how a joke acquired the power to extract one.

The immediate cause was an examination. In May, the paper for India’s national medical entrance test was leaked and sold in advance to some of the 2.3 million candidates competing for roughly 130,000 places. It was canceled and re-held six

author: Signe Marie Cold-Ravnkilde
title: What Europe’s migration deals are really buying
content:
The gravestones are barely visible. Scraps of text scratched into wet cement, left to harden in whatever shape they took. Some have no text at all, just a slight rise in the sand, a low dune along the wall at the far edge of the cemetery in Nouadhibou, Mauritania’s second-largest city and its main Atlantic port, where the Sahara meets the sea. The representative from the municipality walks ahead of us, pointing towards the fringes where the unidentified are buried. Bodies too decomposed to name by the time they reached shore. He has requested a new cemetery, 25km out of town. They are running out of space.

Pirogues on the beach in Nouakchott. Photo by Ahlam Chemlali, March 2026.

We are still standing there when three cars pull up. A battered red Mercedes, followed by two gendarmes in green uniforms who nod at the municipal representative. On an orange stretcher, a white plastic body bag, slightly open. A body has just arrived. The men who came in the cars are from the community — here to try to identify it.

This is what the European Union’s migration partnerships look like from the ground.

author: Markus V. Hoehne
title: Why the US should not recognize Somaliland
content:
Steven A. Cook argues in a recent piece on 

“Why the United States Should Recognize Somaliland”

 that the main reason for recognizing Somaliland is geostrategic. The stakes at play are “confronting the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] and the Houthis as well as shoring up freedom of navigation” (through the Strait of Hormuz and, by extension, the Red Sea and the Suez Canal). He mentions in his account that besides many positive aspects, there were some problems in Somaliland. Concretely, he stresses that “there is opposition to the government among some clans, especially in the east, where sentiment runs in favor of ties with Mogadishu rather than Hargeisa — Somaliland’s capital. This raises the possibility of violent inter-clan conflict in Somaliland. It is a legitimate concern. The good news is that [Somaliland’s President] Irro says he is committed to peaceful dialogue.” This is quite naïve, or willingly ignores the more complex facts. The opposition of those clans in the east is 

long-standing

. Somaliland actually never really controlled the eastern territories, except Lasanod from 2007 to 2022. Armed rebellion emerged there as early as 2009, and in 2023 the militias of the clans in the east defeated the Somaliland army. author: Gathanga Ndung’u
title: This book was born in the streets
content:
Often, history is written as a recollection of the past. It is treated as the entry of passive data, only to be archived for posterity. But what happens when history, or its making, runs parallel to its archival process?

This is the opportunity offered by the 

2024–2025 youth uprisings

 in Kenya. They gave us room to make history, to analyze events as they unfolded daily, and to document them at the same time. However, proper analysis and recourse were insufficient to help tilt the scale from the state to the masses.

Nevertheless, the documentation of the contestations between the masses and the machinery of the state has been extensive. They have been documented in music, memes, spoken word, poems, graffiti, murals, and essays such as our recent scrapbook titled 

From Mau Mau to Ruto Must Go

.

As a contribution to the struggle, 

From Mau Mau to Ruto Must Go

 collects essays from an intergenerational tapestry of activists, community organizers, writers, and legal minds. It is a conversation between the old and the new, produced in the trenches of the youth uprisings, forging an intergenerational continuum of resistance.

The question of sovereignty appears in all the discussions in 

From Mau Mau to Ruto Must Go

. From the streets to the book, external interference in the country’s affairs has been a constant reminder of the incomplete independence we gained in 1963.
